accuracy.reason: Slide 4 teaches the material false guarantee that deletion cancels every in-flight fill and ensures all later reads are fresh. The linked source explicitly disclaims cache-aside consistency; the packet question supplies a direct counterexample.

evidence.quote: Commit the database update, then delete the cache key. This guarantees every later read sees the new value, even if another reader was already filling the cache.
Deletion cancels every in-flight cache fill, so concurrency cannot bring back an old value.

decisions.reason: Reuse, local/shared costs, bounded fallback and when not to cache are usable. However the write policy is falsely advertised as universally fresh; this is separately a hard failure and must be corrected before the decision guidance is safe overall.

evidence.quote: A cache outage can turn most reads into database traffic. Limit fallback work to what the database can handle; reject excess requests or serve older data only where the product rules permit it.
If requests rarely reuse results, or freshness is too hard to maintain, the cache may cost more than it saves.

clarity.reason: Most terms have compact concrete definitions and a consistent example. The faulty guarantee is plainly worded, which increases its risk; readable prose cannot rescue its correctness.

evidence.quote: The API checks and fills the cache explicitly. The cache does not fetch the product from the database on its own.
Sets how long an entry may remain before it expires. A 60-second TTL does not refresh the product every minute; a later miss must load it again.

Slides 1-3 support these steps. Enumerating the lookup plus database read and store recognizes the miss work and extra cache operations without requiring a preferred cost phrase.

The learner correctly traces old hours, later reinsertion, rejection of the guarantee and direct-source bypass using the question and prerequisites. But slide 4 explicitly teaches the opposite of the crucial race and guarantee criteria. Quoting that contradiction does not make the deck support the answer, so this transfer outcome is not taught.

Slides 2 and 5 support entry lifetime, lack of synchronization/residency guarantees and eviction for space. The described fetch on the subsequent request, together with no automatic refresh, distinguishes removal from loading.

Slides 2 and 6 support the reasoning and the learner expressly rejects automatic freshness.

All five criteria satisfied through the complete cap-and-reject response: concurrent misses duplicate reads; one in-progress lookup shares results; outage fallback could redirect 10,000 reads/s to a 500-read/s database; a global 500-read/s cap rejects excess without source work. Slide 7 teaches these mechanisms. The optional old-copy suggestion is conditional on accessibility, not required for this response to work; no stale-copy dependency or unavailable-cache read is assumed.

All five criteria satisfied: no cache now; a post-read fill has no future consumer; the given latency/capacity headroom shows no performance problem; writes and copy management are concrete costs; repeated reads prompt reconsideration with latency/load measurement rather than automatic adoption. Slides 1 and 8 support this reasoning.

hardFailures: Material false freshness guarantee on slide 4: commit-then-delete does not cancel previously started cache fills or ensure every later read is fresh.
The invalidation objective is taught incorrectly: an already fetched old value can be stored after deletion. The learner repairs this from the question despite the lesson.

sourceChecks.claim: Reusable copies reduce repeated source work; Microsoft supports reuse and retaining authoritative data outside the cache.
Hit/miss API ownership matches Microsoft cache-aside steps; its consistency warning supports potentially stale hits.
Microsoft keyspace and cache-aside sections support distinguishing results and explicit application fills.
Every-later-read freshness is false: Microsoft disclaims consistency; the specified later stale fill defeats deletion.
Deletion cancelling in-flight fills is unsupported and false; separate application fills can follow removal.
Redis documents memory eviction, LRU and noeviction rejection, including eviction of keys with remaining TTL. Expiration does not itself fetch source data.
AWS describes independent local copies and external shared entries, with network, operational and availability costs; no automatic database freshness.
AWS supports coalescing duplicate misses, capping source traffic, load shedding and testing unavailable caches. Old-copy service requires an accessible copy.
Microsoft ties caching benefits to repeated costly reads and warns that synchronization overhead can outweigh benefits.
